items.stem:
Read the following extract from a science-fiction short story.

In 2087 you could sell your memories. Most people sold the boring ones first – queues, commutes, tax forms. The MemoryBank paid well for those; rich people used them to feel ordinary.

items.stem:
Read the following "How Doth the Little Crocodile" by Lewis Carroll (1865), a parody of Isaac Watts's "How doth the little busy bee" (1715).

How doth the little crocodile
Improve his shining tail,
And pour the waters of the Nile
On every golden scale!

How cheerfully he seems to grin,
How neatly spreads his claws,
And welcomes little fishes in
With gently smiling jaws!

Explain how this text uses parody or intertextual reference.
items.answer: Carroll's poem parodies Isaac Watts's moral poem for children, which begins "How doth the little busy bee / Improve each shining hour" and praises hard work. Carroll keeps the form and opening but replaces the virtuous bee with a crocodile that "welcomes" fish into its jaws, mocking the preachy moral verse Victorian children had to memorise.

Carroll keeps the form and opening but replaces the virtuous bee with a crocodile that "welcomes" fish into its jaws, mocking the preachy moral verse Victorian children had to memorise. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). items.answer: Indicative content: a mock-serious headline; an absurd but recognisable premise; ironic quotations; exaggeration; a clear target; consistent deadpan tone.

Mark against criteria B, C and D: purpose and audience addressed (C), conventions of the form and logical organisation (B), register, vocabulary and accuracy (D).

items.stem: "Parody is a lazy form of creativity because it borrows from others." Discuss.
items.answer: Parody is a sophisticated creative form: it requires understanding the original and transforming it purposefully.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it relies on existing texts; it may not create original ideas. Arguments against: transforming a source requires skill and insight; many classics are parodies or rewritings. Supported judgement: Parody is a sophisticated creative form: it requires understanding the original and transforming it purposefully. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criteria (each 0-8, scaled to this item). A Analysing: explains content, context, language, structure, technique and style and their effects; justifies opinions with examples and explanation, using terminology. B Organising: a clear, logical structure suited to the task; ideas linked with purpose; referencing conventions. C Producing text: insight, imagination and personal engagement; deliberate stylistic choices; relevant detail and examples. D Using language: varied, accurate vocabulary, sentence structures and forms of expression; appropriate register and style; accurate grammar, spelling and punctuation. 7-8 perceptive/excellent; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate; 1-2 limited.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "deadpan".
items.answer: A serious, expressionless delivery of something absurd, which increases the humour
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a serious, expressionless delivery of something absurd, which increases the humour. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "political cartoon".
items.answer: A drawing that comments on current events or society, often using caricature and symbols

items.stem: Distinguish between allusion and parody.
items.answer: A parody imitates the form and style of a whole text to mock it; an allusion is a brief reference to another text without imitating it.
items.markingKey: A parody imitates the form and style of a whole text to mock it; an allusion is a brief reference to another text without imitating it. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why exaggeration is effective in satire.
items.answer: Pushing a real tendency to an extreme reveals its flaws more clearly – banning thinking exposes a focus on test scores.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Pushing a real tendency to an extreme reveals its flaws more clearly – banning thinking exposes a focus on test scores. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why satire uses humour rather than direct criticism.
items.answer: Humour makes criticism entertaining and memorable, lowers the audience's defences and can expose powerful people safely.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Humour makes criticism entertaining and memorable, lowers the audience's defences and can expose powerful people safely. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "Irony just means a coincidence." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Irony is a gap between appearance and reality, or words and meaning; a coincidence is not necessarily ironic.
items.markingKey: Irony is a gap between appearance and reality, or words and meaning; a coincidence is not necessarily ironic. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the following satirical article from a student humour website.

SCHOOL BANS THINKING TO IMPROVE TEST SCORES
Greenfield Academy has announced a ban on independent thought, after research showed that students who think 'take too long' to fill in multiple-choice answers.
"Curiosity is a distraction," said Head of Results Ms Graves. "Our students don't need to understand. They need to tick."
Questions will now be permitted only on Fridays, between 2:14 and 2:16 p.m.
Parents have welcomed the news. "My son used to ask 'Why?' all the time," said one father. "Now he just says 'Which box?'"

How would you describe the writer's tone? Refer to two language choices that create it.
items.answer: The tone is mock-serious: the straight-faced news style presents an absurd idea as normal.
items.markingKey: The tone is mock-serious: the straight-faced news style presents an absurd idea as normal. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Irony is too subtle to be an effective way of criticising society."
items.answer: Irony risks being misunderstood, but when signalled clearly it is a powerful, memorable form of criticism.

items.stem: "Satire can change people's behaviour." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Satire can raise awareness and shift attitudes, but it rarely changes behaviour on its own; its power lies in starting conversations.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it exposes hypocrisy and makes people think; historical satire has influenced public debate. Arguments against: audiences may laugh without changing; people often enjoy satire that confirms their views. How does the parody use the conventions of advertising to criticise beauty culture?
Write one analytical paragraph (point, evidence, explanation) that answers this question, using at least two quotations.
items.answer: The parody copies real advertising conventions – a glossy product shot, a problem question, ticked benefits, a trademark and a slogan – so readers recognise the genre. Exaggeration exposes the hidden message: the ticked list moves from freckles to "opinions and personality", and the side effects list loss of self. The twisted slogan "Because you're worth nothing... until you're PERFECT™" alludes to real cosmetic slogans and reveals how they sell insecurity.

Exaggeration exposes the hidden message: the ticked list moves from freckles to "opinions and personality", and the side effects list loss of self. The twisted slogan "Because you're worth nothing... until you're PERFECT™" alludes to real cosmetic slogans and reveals how they sell insecurity.
